newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak c.bank says sees C/A deficit at 5 pct of GDP.
newsitem.headline: Slovak c.bank says sees C/A deficit at 5 pct of GDP.

text.p: A slowdown in economic growth in 1997 should help push Slovakia's current account deficit down to about five percent of GDP, National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) Governor Vladimir Masar said.

"In our monetary programme we consider slower GDP growth in 1997, at around five percent year-on-year, as appropriate for our goal of a stable monetary enviroment," Masar said in Thursday's edition of the Slovak Chamber of Industry and Trade bulletin.
"This growth, in which we do not expect significant structural changes from last year, should lower the current account deficit to about five percent (of GDP)," he added.
Masar said that this development of both GDP and the current account should be accompanied by stable foreign exchange and monetary regimes and by a regulated increase of the country's foreign debt.
Slovak real GDP grew 6.9 percent, year-on-year, in 1996, one of the fastest in post-communist Europe, after a 6.8 percent real increase in 1995.
The 1996 current account recorded a $1.94 billion deficit, accounting for more than 10 percent of the country's GDP. The current account was in surplus of $391 million in 1995.

The 1997 budget -- forecast to record a deficit of 36.9 billion crowns, after a 25.5 billion crown shortfall in 1995 -- is based on an assumption that real GDP will grow by 6.4 percent, year-on-year, totalling some 660 billion crowns.
Growth in 1996 was led by domestic demand, creating an increase in the current account deficit and external indebtness, Masar said.
Gross foreign debt rose by around $2 billion last year, a 35 percent increase year-on-year, totalling $7.8 billion at the end of 1996.
"If GDP and its structure show a positive trend, and if foreign trade improves in 1997 the NBS is ready to support this development with its monetary policy," Masar said without further elaboration.

He said he expected the current turbulent situation on the interbank market, where rates have jumped to record levels of above 26 percent several times due to liquidity shortages, to gradually stabilise. He did not say when the situation would change.
